lessons.title: Powder Coatings: Manufacturing and Application
lessons.body:
Powder coatings are 100% solid systemsâno solventâso they cut volatile organic compounds (VOCs) to near zero. In Africa, they are popular for metal furniture, automotive parts, and architectural aluminium. Manufacturing starts with mixing resin (usually polyester or epoxy), pigments, fillers, and additives in a high-speed mixer. The mix is then melt-compounded in an extruder at 90â110Â°C, cooled on a chill roll, and broken into chips. Those chips are ground in a hammer mill or air-classifying mill to an average particle size of 30â50 microns. You need a sieve to check that 98% passes through a 100-mesh screen. Store powder in a cool, dry placeâhumidity above 60% causes clumping.

Application requires a clean, grounded metal substrate. Pre-treatment is critical: degrease with an alkaline cleaner, rinse, and phosphate (iron or zinc) to improve adhesion. For outdoor use, chromate conversion coating gives better corrosion resistance. The powder is applied with an electrostatic spray gun: the gun charges particles to 60â100 kV, and the grounded part attracts them. A typical film thickness is 60â80 microns. Too thin gives poor coverage; too thick causes orange peel.

Curing happens in an oven at 180â200Â°C for 10â15 minutes (metal temperature). Overcuring yellows whites and weakens impact resistance. Undercuring gives poor chemical resistance. In Africa, power fluctuations can ruin a batchâuse a generator or a well-insulated oven. A simple cure test: wipe with methyl ethyl ketone (MEK) 50 times; if the coating softens, it's undercured.

Powder coating is cost-effective for medium-to-high volume production. A small setup in Kenya or Nigeria can start with a manual gun, a batch oven, and a vibratory sieve for under $15,000. Reclaim overspray to save 20â30% material. Always wear a dust mask and ground yourself to avoid static shocks.

lessons.title: UV-Curable Coatings
lessons.body:
UV-curable coatings cure in seconds when exposed to ultraviolet lightâno heat, no solvent. They are ideal for wood, plastic, and metal in Africa where electricity is unreliable because they need only a lamp, not a large oven. The formulation has three main parts: oligomers (epoxy acrylate, urethane acrylate), monomers (dilvents like TPGDA), and photoinitiators (e.g., Irgacure 184). Pigments and additives (flow agents, defoamers) complete the mix. Mix in a dark room or under yellow light to prevent premature curing.

Manufacturing is simple: blend oligomer and monomer at 40â60Â°C, add photoinitiator (2â5% by weight), then pigment. Use a high-speed disperser for 20â30 minutes. Check viscosity with a Ford cupâtarget 20â30 seconds for spray, 100â150 seconds for roller. Store in opaque containers away from sunlight. A 20-litre batch can be made in a stainless steel pot with a mechanical stirrer.

Application: spray, roller, or curtain coat. For wood, sand to 180â220 grit, apply 80â120 g/mÂ², then cure under a medium-pressure mercury lamp (80â120 W/cm) at a line speed of 5â10 m/min. The lamp must be 10â15 cm from the surface. Cure dose is typically 500â1000 mJ/cmÂ². If the coating feels tacky after curing, increase lamp power or add more photoinitiator. For pigmented coatings, use a gallium-doped lamp for deeper penetration.

UV coatings give high gloss, scratch resistance, and fast turnaround. In Africa, they are used for furniture, flooring, and plastic parts. Safety: UV light damages eyes and skinâuse shielding and goggles. Never look directly at the lamp. Ventilate the area because monomers can irritate. A basic UV line with a conveyor and one lamp costs about $8,000â$12,000.

lessons.title: High-Solids and Waterborne Coatings
lessons.body:
High-solids and waterborne coatings reduce solvent emissions and are increasingly required in Africa for factory-applied finishes. High-solids coatings have more than 70% solid content by weight. They use low-viscosity resins (e.g., acrylic, polyester) and reactive diluents. The trade-off: higher viscosity means you need powerful mixers and precise thinning. A typical formulation: 50% resin, 20% pigment, 25% filler, 5% additives. Mix in a high-speed disperser at 1,500 rpm for 30 minutes, then let it sit for 24 hours to de-aerate. Apply with airless spray at 150â200 bar. Film thickness 50â75 microns. Cure at 120â150Â°C for 20 minutes.

Waterborne coatings use water as the main carrier. They contain resin emulsion (acrylic, styrene-acrylic), pigments, coalescing agents (e.g., Texanol), and biocides. Manufacturing: disperse pigment in water with a dispersant, then add emulsion slowly under low shear (300â500 rpm) to avoid breaking the emulsion. Adjust pH to 8â9 with ammonia. Viscosity target: 80â100 KU (Krebs units). Apply by brush, roller, or spray. Drying at ambient temperature (25â30Â°C) takes 1â2 hours touch-dry, 7 days full cure. In humid African climates, add 1â2% coalescent to help film formation.

Waterborne coatings are user-friendly, low odour, and clean up with water. But they can rust steel cansâuse plastic or lined containers. High-solids need good ventilation because solvents are still present. For a small factory, a waterborne line is cheaper: a 500-litre stainless steel tank, a low-shear mixer, and a pH meter cost under $5,000. Test adhesion with a cross-hatch cutter and tape pull. Both types are gaining ground in Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa due to environmental regulations.

lessons.title: Anti-Corrosive and Marine Coatings
lessons.body:
Africaâs long coastline and humid climate make anti-corrosive and marine coatings essential for ships, oil rigs, bridges, and pipelines. These coatings protect steel from rust and saltwater. The key is a three-part system: primer, intermediate, and topcoat. Primer: zinc-rich epoxy (80% zinc by weight) gives cathodic protection. Mix zinc dust with epoxy resin just before useâpot life is 4â8 hours. Apply 75â100 microns wet film. Intermediate: high-build epoxy (150â200 microns) for barrier protection. Topcoat: polyurethane or silicone for UV and colour stability.

Surface preparation is 80% of the job. Blast clean to Sa 2.5 (near-white metal) with a profile of 50â75 microns. In humid areas, apply primer within 4 hours of blasting to avoid flash rust. Use a wet film gauge and magnetic dry film gauge to check thickness. For marine environments, total dry film thickness should be 250â350 microns. Apply with airless spray or brush for small areas. Overcoating windows: epoxy can be recoated after 6â24 hours at 25Â°C; if longer, sand to create a key.

Formulation tips: add anti-corrosive pigments like zinc phosphate (5â10%) or micaceous iron oxide (MIO) for barrier. For splash zones, use glass flake epoxy. In Africa, local fillers like talc and barytes can reduce cost, but never substitute zinc in the primer. Test salt spray resistance: ASTM B117 for 500â1000 hours. A simple field test: immerse a coated panel in seawater for 3 months and check for blisters.

Safety: zinc dust is flammableâkeep away from sparks. Epoxy hardeners cause skin sensitisationâwear nitrile gloves and long sleeves. A small marine coating operation can start with a blast pot, airless sprayer, and mixing station for under $20,000. Maintenance schedules are critical: inspect every 6 months and touch up damaged areas immediately.

lessons.title: Fire-Retardant and Intumescent Coatings
lessons.body:
Fire-retardant coatings slow flame spread; intumescent coatings swell when heated to form an insulating char. In Africa, they are used on steel structures, wooden buildings, and electrical cables. Intumescent coatings contain three key ingredients: acid source (ammonium polyphosphate), carbon source (pentaerythritol), and blowing agent (melamine). When heated above 200Â°C, they react to form a thick foam (20â50 times original thickness) that insulates the substrate. Mix these powders with a binder (acrylic or epoxy) and solvent or water. A typical formulation: 20% APP, 10% pentaerythritol, 8% melamine, 40% binder, 22% additives and pigment. Disperse in a high-speed mixer for 30 minutes; check fineness with a Hegman gauge (target 4â6).

Application: for steel, apply 0.5â2.0 mm dry film thickness depending on fire rating (30, 60, or 120 minutes). Use airless spray or trowel. Cure at ambient or with gentle heat (60Â°C). Test with a propane torch: the coating should char and swell, not drip. For wood, use a clear intumescent varnish (e.g., based on melamine phosphate) at 200â300 g/mÂ². In Africa, humidity can affect curingâadd a biocide to waterborne versions.

Fire-retardant coatings (non-intumescent) use additives like antimony trioxide, aluminium hydroxide, or brominated compounds. They are cheaper but less effective. For cables, use a halogen-free retardant to avoid toxic smoke. Always check local fire codesâmany African countries follow British (BS) or European (EN) standards. A simple burn test: hold a coated panel in a flame for 10 seconds; the flame should not spread beyond the charred area.

Safety: these coatings may contain borates or phosphatesâwear a dust mask. Store in a dry place. A small production setup: a ribbon blender, a three-roll mill, and a spray booth. Cost per litre is higher than standard paint, but the life-saving benefit justifies it. Train workers on fire safety and keep a CO2 extinguisher nearby.

lessons.title: Smart and Functional Coatings
lessons.body:
Smart coatings respond to their environmentâthey change colour, self-heal, or release chemicals on demand. In Africa, they are emerging in niche markets: temperature-indicating paints for cold chains, self-healing coatings for pipelines, and anti-fouling coatings for boats. A simple smart coating: thermochromic paint that changes from coloured to clear at 30Â°C. Formulation: mix leuco dye (e.g., crystal violet lactone), developer (bisphenol A), and solvent (1-tetradecanol) in a ratio of 1:2:20. Encapsulate the mixture in melamine-formaldehyde microcapsules (5â10 microns), then add to a water-based paint at 5â10% by weight. Apply by brush; when temperature rises, the coating turns clear.

Self-healing coatings use microcapsules filled with healing agent (e.g., linseed oil or dicyclopentadiene). When scratched, capsules break and release the agent, which cures with a catalyst in the coating. For epoxy systems, use Grubbs catalyst. In Africa, a simpler self-healing approach: add 5% linseed oil microcapsules to alkyd paintâwhen damaged, oil oxidises and fills the scratch. Test by scratching with a knife and observing after 24 hours.

Anti-fouling coatings for boats use copper oxide (Cu2O) or zinc pyrithione. Biocide release rate should be 5â10 Âµg/cmÂ²/day. Mix 20â40% Cu2O in a rosin/acrylic binder. Apply 100â150 microns. In African coastal waters, fouling is aggressiveâreapply every 12â18 months. Functional coatings also include conductive paints (silver-coated copper particles for EMI shielding) and photocatalytic coatings (titanium dioxide for self-cleaning).

Manufacturing smart coatings requires precision: use a bead mill for microcapsule dispersion, and avoid high shear that breaks capsules. Store below 30Â°C. A small lab setup: a magnetic stirrer, a microscope to check capsules, and a drawdown bar for films. Safety: some smart materials are expensive and sensitive to moistureâkeep containers sealed. Start with one product, like thermochromic paint for coffee cups, and scale up. The market is growing in South Africa and Kenya for innovative, high-value coatings.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Specialty Coatings & Advanced Formulations for African Paint Manufacturers

This practical reference consolidates the technical and commercial essentials of six specialty coating families: powder coatings, UV-curable coatings, high-solids and waterborne coatings, anti-corrosive and marine coatings, fire-retardant and intumescent coatings, and smart/functional coatings. For an African paint manufacturer, the strategic question is not whether these technologies are technically superior â it is whether they can be produced, applied, and sold profitably within local supply chains, climate conditions, and regulatory frameworks. This module treats each family through that lens: raw material access, capital intensity, application requirements, and market demand across African construction, marine, mining, and infrastructure sectors.

1. Powder Coatings: Manufacturing and Application

Powder coatings are 100% solid systems â no solvent, no VOC at application. The manufacturing process involves dry blending resins (typically polyester, epoxy, or hybrid), pigments, fillers, and additives, followed by melt-mixing in an extruder, cooling, flaking, and grinding to a controlled particle size (typically 10â100 Âµm). Application is via electrostatic spray onto grounded metal substrates, then curing in an oven at 160â200Â°C for 10â20 minutes.

Africa context: Powder coating lines are capital-intensive (extruder, grinder, electrostatic guns, curing oven). The business case is strongest where there is concentrated demand: appliance manufacturing in Egypt and South Africa, architectural aluminium for windows and facades in Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana, and automotive components in South Africa and Morocco. The key barrier is not formulation knowledge but access to consistent resin supply and reliable electricity for curing ovens. Manufacturers serving the architectural aluminium sector â a growing market driven by urban construction â can justify the investment through long-run contracts with fabricators.

2. UV-Curable Coatings

UV-curable coatings cure instantly when exposed to ultraviolet light (typically 200â400 nm) in the presence of photoinitiators. Formulations are 100% solids (or high-solids), containing oligomers (epoxy acrylates, urethane acrylates), reactive diluents (monomers), photoinitiators, and additives. Cure times are measured in seconds, enabling high-throughput production lines with minimal floor space.

Africa context: UV curing is best suited to factory-based applications: wood panel finishing, plastic coatings, graphic arts, and flooring. The technology is less practical for field application (no UV source) and for thick or pigmented films where light penetration is limited. For African manufacturers, the opportunity lies in supplying furniture and board manufacturers in Egypt, South Africa, and Nigeria, where UV lines are already installed. The main constraint is the cost and import dependency of photoinitiators and specialty oligomers.

3. High-Solids and Waterborne Coatings

High-solids coatings contain 60â85% volume solids, reducing solvent emissions per unit area. Waterborne coatings use water as the primary carrier, with resin dispersions (acrylic, polyurethane, alkyd hybrids) and coalescing agents. Both families respond to tightening VOC regulations and workplace safety requirements.

Africa context: Waterborne architectural coatings already dominate the African decorative market (emulsion paints). The growth opportunity is in industrial and protective waterborne systems â direct-to-metal acrylics, waterborne epoxies, and waterborne polyurethanes â which are gaining traction in South Africa, Kenya, and Nigeria as VOC enforcement and worker safety concerns increase. High-solids solventborne systems remain important for heavy-duty protective coatings where waterborne performance is still catching up. African manufacturers should invest in waterborne resin dispersion technology and coalescing agent optimization to reduce dependence on imported finished paints.

4. Anti-Corrosive and Marine Coatings

Anti-corrosive coatings protect steel and concrete from electrochemical degradation. Key technologies include epoxy primers (barrier protection), zinc-rich primers (cathodic protection), polyurethane topcoats (UV and chemical resistance), and glass-flake or ceramic-filled systems for aggressive environments. Marine coatings add antifouling, abrasion resistance, and seawater immersion performance.

Africa context: This is arguably the highest-value specialty segment for African manufacturers. The continent has extensive marine infrastructure (ports in Durban, Lagos, Mombasa, Tema, Abidjan), mining operations (South Africa, DRC, Zambia, Ghana), oil and gas facilities (Nigeria, Angola, Mozambique), and corrosion-prone coastal construction. The challenge is that high-performance anti-corrosive systems often require zinc dust, epoxy resins, and polyamine curing agents that are imported. Local manufacturing can compete on formulation, blending, and application services rather than raw material production. A business-first strategy: partner with mining and port operators on long-term maintenance contracts rather than selling paint as a commodity.

5. Fire-Retardant and Intumescent Coatings

Fire-retardant coatings reduce flame spread and heat release. Intumescent coatings are a subset that expand under heat to form an insulating char layer, protecting structural steel and timber. Formulations typically contain an acid source (ammonium polyphosphate), a carbon source (pentaerythritol), a blowing agent (melamine), and a binder resin. They are tested to standards such as EN 13381-8, ASTM E119, or BS 476.

Africa context: Demand is driven by building codes, insurance requirements, and high-rise construction in South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, and Egypt. The market is small but high-margin, and certification is a major barrier â testing is expensive and often requires sending samples to accredited labs in Europe or South Africa. African manufacturers should consider licensing formulations or partnering with certified international producers rather than developing from scratch.

6. Smart and Functional Coatings

Smart coatings respond to external stimuli â self-healing (microcapsules release healing agents), anti-bacterial (silver or copper nanoparticles), self-cleaning (photocatalytic TiOâ), and thermal-regulating (phase-change materials). Functional coatings include conductive, anti-static, and anti-graffiti systems.

Africa context: The most commercially viable smart coating for Africa is anti-bacterial and self-cleaning for healthcare, food processing, and public infrastructure. Photocatalytic TiOâ coatings for concrete facades are gaining interest in polluted urban environments. However, the technology is still largely imported, and local manufacturing requires nanoparticle handling capability and significant R&D investment. The business-first approach is to import the active ingredients and formulate locally for specific applications â hospitals, schools, and food plants.

Data Tables

Table 1: Comparison of Specialty Coating Technologies for African Manufacturers

UV-Curable Low to zero Medium Photoinitiators, oligomers Furniture, flooring, plastics

Source: Author's synthesis based on European Coatings Handbook (3rd ed., Vincentz Network, 2018) and African market data from Frost & Sullivan, African Paints and Coatings Market Report, 2022.

Table 2: Estimated Raw Material Cost Share by Coating Type

Anti-Corrosive 35â45% 35â45% (zinc) 10â20% High (zinc, epoxy)

Source: Adapted from Paint and Coatings Industry: Raw Material Cost Analysis, American Coatings Association, 2021, and industry interviews conducted in South Africa and Nigeria, 2023.

â  SAFETY WARNING â HIGH-RISK FORMULATION COMPONENTS

Powder coating manufacture generates combustible dust â fine resin and pigment particles can form explosive atmospheres. UV-curable formulations contain reactive acrylate monomers that are skin sensitizers and potential carcinogens; avoid skin contact and ensure adequate ventilation. Intumescent coatings release ammonia and phosphorus-based gases during fire exposure and must be applied with respiratory protection. Zinc-rich primers contain zinc dust which is harmful if inhaled and reacts with acids to release hydrogen. Anti-fouling marine coatings may contain biocides regulated under the IMO Anti-Fouling Systems Convention. In all cases, comply with local occupational health regulations and provide appropriate PPE, dust extraction, and fume hoods. African manufacturers should conduct a full risk assessment before commencing production of any specialty coating.

Quick Reference Checklist for African Manufacturers

  1. Assess raw material access first. Before committing to a specialty coating line, confirm that resins, curing agents, and pigments can be sourced reliably â or that local substitutes exist.
  2. Match technology to application infrastructure. Powder and UV coatings require factory-based curing equipment; do not attempt field application without the right hardware.
  3. Calculate total landed cost, not just formulation cost. Import duties, freight, and currency volatility can double the effective cost of specialty raw materials.
  4. Target high-value sectors with long-term contracts. Mining, ports, oil and gas, and high-rise construction offer repeat business and higher margins than commodity decorative paints.
  5. Invest in application training. Specialty coatings fail more often from poor surface preparation and application than from formulation error.
  6. Verify regulatory compliance early. VOC limits, fire certification, and biocide regulations differ by country â check before formulating.
  7. Partner for certification. Intumescent and marine coatings require accredited testing; partner with certified labs or license proven formulations.
  8. Start with waterborne and high-solids. These offer the lowest capital barrier and the widest market applicability for African manufacturers entering specialty coatings.

Further Reading

  • US EPA Safer Choice â Safer Chemical Ingredients List (free access to chemical safety data relevant to coating formulation)
  • ISO 12944-5:2019 â Corrosion Protection of Steel Structures by Protective Paint Systems (standard reference for anti-corrosive systems)
  • AMPP (Association for Materials Protection and Performance) â free technical resources on corrosion and protective coatings
  • African Coatings Journal â regional market intelligence and technical articles for African manufacturers
  • ILO Occupational Safety and Health â Chemical Safety (free guidance on handling coating raw materials safely)

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills programme. For practical workshops, raw material sourcing contacts, and business plan templates, contact your regional Rise Africa training partner.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of powder coatings over solvent-based paints?
options: C) They can be applied by brush
D) They are cheaper than all other coatings
quiz.explanation: Powder coatings contain no solvent, so they emit almost no volatile organic compounds.

quiz.q: What is the typical particle size of powder coating after grinding?
quiz.explanation: Powder coatings are ground to an average particle size of 30â50 microns for good electrostatic spray application.

quiz.q: Which pre-treatment step is critical for powder coating adhesion?
quiz.explanation: Degreasing and phosphating clean the metal and improve powder adhesion and corrosion resistance.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for powder coating cure?
quiz.explanation: Wiping with methyl ethyl ketone (MEK) 50 times checks if the coating is properly cured; if it softens, it's undercured.

quiz.q: What is the main component of UV-curable coatings that initiates curing?
quiz.explanation: Photoinitiators absorb UV light and generate free radicals that start the polymerisation reaction.

quiz.q: Why should UV-curable coatings be mixed under yellow light?
quiz.explanation: Yellow light filters out UV wavelengths, preventing the photoinitiator from triggering curing during mixing.

quiz.q: What is a typical cure dose for UV coatings?
quiz.explanation: UV coatings typically require a cure dose of 500â1000 mJ/cmÂ² for proper crosslinking.

quiz.q: What is the solid content by weight of high-solids coatings?
quiz.explanation: High-solids coatings are defined as having more than 70% solid content by weight.

quiz.q: What is a common coalescing agent for waterborne coatings?
quiz.explanation: Texanol is a widely used coalescing agent that helps waterborne films form properly at ambient temperatures.

quiz.q: What pH should waterborne coatings be adjusted to?
quiz.explanation: Waterborne coatings are typically adjusted to pH 8â9 with ammonia for stability and proper viscosity.

quiz.q: Why should waterborne coatings not be stored in unlined steel cans?
options: A) They react with steel to cause rust
quiz.explanation: Water in the coating can rust unlined steel cans, contaminating the product.

quiz.q: What is the function of zinc-rich primer in anti-corrosive coatings?
quiz.explanation: Zinc particles sacrificially protect steel by acting as an anode, preventing rust.

quiz.q: What surface preparation standard is required for marine coatings?
quiz.explanation: Sa 2.5 (near-white metal blast cleaning) is the standard for marine anti-corrosive coatings.

quiz.q: What is the total dry film thickness for a marine coating system?
quiz.explanation: Marine environments require a total dry film thickness of 250â350 microns for adequate protection.

quiz.q: Which pigment is commonly used as an anti-corrosive in primers?
quiz.explanation: Zinc phosphate is an anti-corrosive pigment that passivates steel and improves adhesion.

quiz.q: What is the main safety hazard when handling zinc dust?
options: C) It is toxic by inhalation
quiz.explanation: Zinc dust is flammable and can cause explosions if not kept away from sparks or flames.

quiz.q: What are the three key ingredients in an intumescent coating?
options: A) Acid source, carbon source, blowing agent
quiz.explanation: Intumescent coatings require an acid source (e.g., ammonium polyphosphate), a carbon source (e.g., pentaerythritol), and a blowing agent (e.g., melamine).

quiz.q: At what temperature does an intumescent coating typically start to swell?
quiz.explanation: Intumescent coatings react above 200Â°C to form an insulating char.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test for fire-retardant coatings?
quiz.explanation: Holding a coated panel in a flame for 10 seconds shows if the flame spreads or self-extinguishes.

quiz.q: Which additive is used in fire-retardant coatings to reduce smoke?
quiz.explanation: Antimony trioxide acts as a synergist with halogenated flame retardants to reduce smoke and improve flame resistance.

quiz.q: What is a smart coating that changes colour with temperature?
quiz.explanation: Thermochromic coatings change colour in response to temperature changes.

quiz.q: What is the typical size of microcapsules in self-healing coatings?
quiz.explanation: Microcapsules for self-healing coatings are typically 5â10 microns in diameter.

quiz.q: Which biocide is commonly used in anti-fouling coatings?
quiz.explanation: Copper oxide (Cu2O) is a common biocide that prevents marine organisms from attaching to hulls.

quiz.q: What is the release rate of biocide from an anti-fouling coating?
quiz.explanation: Anti-fouling coatings typically release biocide at 5â10 Âµg/cmÂ²/day to be effective without harming the environment excessively.

quiz.q: What is the function of titanium dioxide in photocatalytic coatings?
quiz.explanation: Titanium dioxide in photocatalytic coatings breaks down organic dirt when exposed to UV light, making the surface self-cleaning.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to test self-healing in a coating?
options: A) Scratch it and wait 24 hours
quiz.explanation: Scratching the coating and observing if the scratch fills or heals after 24 hours indicates self-healing ability.

quiz.q: Which of these is a functional coating?
quiz.explanation: Conductive paint is a functional coating that provides electrical conductivity for EMI shielding.

quiz.q: What is a common application for thermochromic coatings in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Thermochromic coatings are used as temperature indicators for vaccines and food in cold chains.

quiz.q: What safety precaution is needed when making smart coatings with microcapsules?
quiz.explanation: High shear can break microcapsules, so gentle mixing is required to preserve their integrity.

quiz.q: Which African countries are mentioned as emerging markets for smart coatings?
quiz.explanation: South Africa and Kenya are noted as growing markets for innovative, high-value smart coatings.
